summary: A best current practice document recording a variance from the normal IETF standards-process procedures so that the PPP Compression Control Protocol and PPP Encryption Control Protocol could move forward.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a game needs a special exception to the usual rule. This note writes down the exception that let two dial-up link protocols continue through the process.

subtitle: An IESG exception that let two PPP protocols advance despite unresolved patent licensing.

tldr.problem: The PPP Compression Control Protocol (CCP) and Encryption Control Protocol (ECP) were stalled because Motorola claimed patents on them and RFC 1602 required a formal license form before they could advance.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG used the variance procedure of RFC 1871 to waive that requirement and accepted Motorola's written statement that licenses will be made available instead.
tldr.outcome: The IESG could adopt CCP and ECP as originally developed. The memo itself names the risk: licenses might not be granted fairly or without discrimination.

today: RFC 1915 is a Best Current Practice record of one variance, and its status is not marked obsoleted or updated. It documents an exception to the procedures of RFC 1602, not a protocol.

sections.title: The Problem: Patents Block Two Protocols
sections.content:
The PPP Working Group developed two protocols. The Compression Control Protocol (CCP) controls compression on PPP links, and the Encryption Control Protocol (ECP) controls encryption on serial links. Both were finished and sent to the IESG for standardization.

During development, Motorola told the IETF that the protocols may infringe its U.S. patents 5,245,614 and 5,130,993. Because of these claims, the protocols' progress was halted.

Under the procedures of RFC 1602, the IESG Secretariat tried to obtain the required licenses, and in particular tried to acquire a form of the license and make it publicly available on the Internet. Motorola preferred a general statement that licenses will be made available to any party under reasonable terms and conditions that are demonstrably free of unfair discrimination.
sections.eli5: Two useful tools were ready, but a company said it owned ideas inside them. The usual paperwork for using such ideas was not finished, so the tools got stuck.

sections.title: Why Redesigning Was Not the Answer
sections.content:
The working group tried to write revised versions of CCP and ECP that would not infringe the patents. This was technically possible, but some members considered the changes much less desirable than the originals. They said they would implement the original CCP regardless of what the working group or the IESG standardized.

Other members accepted the changes, but mostly because it seemed the only viable alternative rather than because of the technical merit. The memo concludes that the technical changes did not reach the IETF's traditional benchmark of Rough Consensus.
sections.eli5: Some kids offered to change the game so nobody owned a piece of it. Others said the new game was worse and they would play the old one anyway, so everyone could not agree.

sections.title: What RFC 1602 Normally Requires
sections.content:
Section 5.6 of RFC 1602 sets three conditions for using proprietary technology in an Internet Standard. The holder must agree to give the ISOC a free license and grant others a license on fair and non-discriminatory terms. A form of this license must be made electronically available on the Internet. And anyone must be able to execute it by downloading the form, meeting its requirements, and mailing an executed copy to the licenser.

Standards track documents are not allowed to advance until these conditions are met. The variance lets CCP and ECP advance without meeting them. The community would get only an assurance from the license holder that it will make licenses available.
sections.eli5: The normal rule asks the owner to put a ready-to-sign permission form where everyone can find it. The exception skips the form and uses a promise instead.

sections.title: The Variance and the Motorola Statement
sections.content:
Using the Variance Procedure published as RFC 1871, the IESG grants a variance on behalf of the PPP Working Group to the procedures of RFC 1602. This allows the IESG to adopt CCP and ECP as originally developed.

The IESG accepts a statement by G. David Forney of Motorola, dated 5 June 1995 and attached as Appendix A, that Motorola will make licenses available to use the technology covered by the two patents. In that email Forney called it most unusual to attach a license agreement to a standard, and proposed a short notice with Motorola's licensing contact instead.
sections.eli5: The coach agrees to the exception and writes down the owner's promise. The owner also says a long form is not usual and suggests just giving out a phone number.

sections.title: Perceived Benefits and Risks
sections.content:
The stated benefit is that the IESG can standardize CCP and ECP, giving the community a standard way to control data compression and encryption on PPP links. The memo argues the need is real because the protocol had been under development for well over a year.

The stated risk is that licenses might not be granted in a fair and non-discriminatory manner. A license holder could treat each request differently, advancing some and delaying others. The memo says this would run counter to the IETF's tradition of openness and equal access to technology.
sections.eli5: The good part is that everyone gets a standard way to squash and scramble data. The worry is that the owner might be nicer to some people than others.

sections.title: The Appendices
sections.content:
Appendix A reproduces the 5 June 1995 email from Forney to Steve Coya, Executive Director of the IETF. It says Motorola has had a license agreement available for some time and has already given it to several requesting companies.

Appendix B quotes section 5.6 of RFC 1602, the assurances agreement that the variance sets aside. Among its terms, the rights holder grants ISOC a cost-free license, and grants members of the Internet community a license for a reasonable royalty. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: At the end, the note attaches the owner's email and a copy of the usual rule, so readers can compare the promise with what was normally required.

references.text: Internet Architecture Board and Internet Engineering Steering Group, "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 2", RFC 1602, March 1994.
